title: Alternative Specimens: Salivary Cortisol, Meconium, β2-Transferrin and Matrix Validation
summary: Learn what late-night saliva, meconium and β2-transferrin each reveal, how to collect and read them, and why any non-serum fluid on a serum assay needs its own validation.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 30 Hits 11, 12 and 14 and Trap 5. Checked against Nieman 2008 (Endocrine Society guideline; read via a page-fetch tool), Lange 2014, Price 2018, Maschke 2021, de Campos 2022, Oh 2017, Normansell 1994 (abstract-level page read via a page-fetch tool) and the Croatian body-fluid recommendations (Milevoj Kopcinovic 2020; Jokic 2020). Hit 14 calls β2-transferrin CSF-specific; Oh 2017 states it is also found in perilymph and vitreous humour, with false positives after eye rupture (register flag rv-b2-transferrin-not-csf-only). Hit 12 gives a 2nd–3rd trimester window; sources put meconium formation at about 12 weeks, some up to 20 weeks, and one cohort used EtG ≥10 ng/g as a third-trimester marker (register flag rv-meconium-window-onset). The CLSI C49-A document itself was not read (not open access); the matrix-validation rule is taught from the Croatian recommendations, which use C49-A as a framework. Two further meconium pages were not used for teaching: Williamson 2006 (PMC2672735, a short report read via a page-fetch tool) and PMC1721515 (blocked by a browser verification page, so not read). Not taught: traumatic-tap correction, postpericardiotomy syndrome, salivary cortisone or assay-specific cut-offs.

objectives: Explain why saliva reflects free cortisol and how late-night salivary cortisol is collected and confounded.
State which part of pregnancy meconium reflects, and its limits compared with neonatal urine.
Recognise where β2-transferrin is found and what can cause a false positive.
Apply the rule that a non-serum fluid on a serum assay needs validation for each fluid type and assay.

scenes.title: Three specimens that are not blood
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three non-blood specimens arrive. (1) Two saliva swabs collected at home late in the evening for a patient with suspected Cushing syndrome. (2) Meconium from a newborn; the mother reports drinking alcohol only in the first weeks of pregnancy, and meconium ethyl glucuronide (EtG) is negative. (3) Clear nasal drip after a head injury, sent to confirm a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak. Question token: “What window does each specimen see?”

cues.text: Three specimens arrive, and none of them is blood: two late-evening saliva swabs for suspected Cushing syndrome, and meconium from a newborn.
The newborn’s mother drank only in early pregnancy, and the meconium test for an alcohol marker is negative. The third specimen is clear nasal drip after a head injury.
Each specimen sees only part of the story. What window does each one see?

props.label: What window does each specimen see?

scenes.title: What each matrix reflects
scenes.altText: Schematic: three specimen cards. Saliva: biologically active free cortisol in blood is in equilibrium with salivary cortisol; drugs in oral fluid are mostly the free (unbound) fraction. Meconium: the first bowel movements; it begins forming around 12 weeks of gestation (some authors say later, up to 20 weeks) as fetal swallowing starts, so it stores exposure from the second and third trimesters and cannot show first-trimester exposure. Neonatal urine is quick and easy but shows only recent maternal use. Beta-2 transferrin: beta-1 transferrin is in serum, tears, nasal secretions and saliva; beta-2 transferrin is found in CSF, perilymph and vitreous humour.

cues.text: Saliva is often described as a filtrate of blood. Free, biologically active cortisol in the blood is in equilibrium with cortisol in saliva, and drugs in oral fluid are mainly the unbound fraction.
Meconium is the newborn’s first stool. It starts forming around twelve weeks of gestation, when the fetus begins swallowing, so it stores exposure from the second and third trimesters, not the first.
Neonatal urine is quick to collect but shows only recent maternal drug use. Meconium gives the longer window.
Transferrin has two forms. Beta-one is in serum, tears, nasal secretions and saliva. Beta-two is found in cerebrospinal fluid, and also in perilymph and the vitreous humour of the eye.

lines: β1 in serum, tears, nose, saliva

scenes.title: Late-night salivary cortisol done right
scenes.altText: Cushing card (Endocrine Society 2008 guideline): loss of the late-night cortisol nadir is a consistent abnormality. Initial testing uses ONE of: urine free cortisol (at least two), late-night salivary cortisol (two measurements), 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, or 2-day low-dose dexamethasone test. Saliva collection: two separate evenings between 2300 and 2400 h. Interference card: avoid smoking on the collection day; licorice (or chewing tobacco) may theoretically raise late-night salivary cortisol; steroid-containing lotions or oral gels contaminating the swab may give false positives. An abnormal result leads to an endocrinologist and a second test; concordant normal results end the work-up.

cues.text: In Cushing syndrome, cortisol loses its normal late-night low point. Saliva collected late in the evening shows whether that low point is missing.

The 2008 Endocrine Society guideline offers late-night salivary cortisol as one of four first tests, along with urine free cortisol, the one-milligram overnight dexamethasone test, and the two-day low-dose test.

For saliva, collect on two separate evenings between eleven and midnight. Avoid smoking that day. Steroid lotions or oral gels on the swab can give false positives, and licorice may, in theory, raise the result.
An abnormal first test means referral to an endocrinologist and a second test. Two normal results end the work-up.

scenes.title: Reading meconium, nasal fluid and any new matrix
scenes.altText: Meconium card: fatty acid ethyl esters (FAEE) above a cumulative cut-point of 2 nmol/g are a validated marker of prenatal alcohol exposure (one study: sensitivity 84.2%, specificity 83.3%); EtG of at least 10 ng/g indicates third-trimester exposure in one cohort. Caveats: meconium can be passed in utero, may contain drugs given during labour, and its passage can be delayed. Beta-2 transferrin card: agarose electrophoresis with antitransferrin immunodetection needs only microlitres of fluid; ruptured eye (vitreous) can give a false positive; one review calls the test costly and slow (an earlier lab report called its 3.5-hour run fast). Matrix card: a serum assay used on another fluid is a method modification — validate for each fluid type and assay; if a matrix effect cannot be excluded, report with a comment on the limitation.

cues.text: Meconium is tested for alcohol markers. Fatty acid ethyl esters above a set cut-point are a validated marker of prenatal alcohol exposure, and in one study ethyl glucuronide at or above ten nanograms per gram was taken to mark third-trimester drinking.
Meconium has limits. It can be passed before birth, it may contain drugs given during labour, and its passage can be delayed.

Beta-two transferrin is detected by electrophoresis with an antitransferrin antibody on microlitres of fluid. A ruptured eye can give a false positive, and one review notes the test is costly and slow to report.
And any non-serum fluid on a serum assay is a method modification. Validate it for each fluid type and assay, and if a matrix effect cannot be excluded, report it with a comment on the limitation.

props.title: New matrix = method modification
lines: Validate per fluid type and assay
Matrix effect? Report with a limitation comment

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Use the serum reference range for any fluid” (✓ validate per fluid type and assay; fluids usually lack reference intervals); “Negative meconium rules out any prenatal exposure” (✓ meconium does not capture first-trimester exposure); “Beta-2 transferrin is found only in CSF” (✓ also perilymph and vitreous humour; eye rupture can give a false positive).

cues.text: Trap one: any fluid can borrow the serum reference range. No: each fluid type and assay needs its own validation, and most fluids have no reference intervals.
Trap two: a negative meconium test rules out prenatal exposure. No: meconium does not capture the first trimester.
Trap three: beta-two transferrin exists only in spinal fluid. No: perilymph and the vitreous humour contain it too.

props.title: ✗ “Serum ranges fit any fluid.”
lines: ✓ Validate per fluid type and assay

scenes.title: Witnesses with windows
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Every specimen is a witness with a window. Saliva saw the FREE cortisol at bedtime; meconium saw the LATER months of pregnancy; beta-2 transferrin saw the fluid around the brain (and ear and eye). No witness is believed until the lab has validated it.” Tokens: saliva = free at night · meconium = after the first trimester · β2 = brain fluid. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: every specimen is a witness with a window. Saliva saw the free cortisol at bedtime. Meconium saw the later months of pregnancy. Beta-two transferrin saw the fluid around the brain. And no witness is believed until the lab has validated it.

Where it breaks: when meconium starts forming is debated, so its window has no sharp start; beta-two transferrin is also in ear and eye fluid; and steroid gels or lotions, and possibly licorice, can make saliva tell a false story.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Saliva = free cortisol, 2 evenings 23:00–24:00 · meconium = 2nd + 3rd trimester · β2-transferrin = CSF, perilymph, vitreous”, “Any non-serum fluid on a serum assay → validate per fluid and assay”.

cues.text: Each alternative specimen has its own window, with saliva showing free cortisol late at night, meconium showing the later months of pregnancy and beta-2 transferrin marking spinal, ear or eye fluid, and none of them may borrow serum reference ranges without validation.

props.label: Saliva = free, 23–24 h · meconium = 2nd + 3rd trim. · β2 = CSF/ear/eye
Non-serum fluid on a serum assay → validate per fluid and assay

explanation.what: Plain language: some lab tests use fluids other than blood. Each fluid only “sees” part of what happens in the body: saliva shows the free hormone at the moment it is collected, a newborn’s first stool collects what the fetus was exposed to in the later months of pregnancy, and a special form of transferrin usually points to the fluid around the brain as the source of a clear leak. A lab cannot simply run these fluids on a blood test and use blood ranges. Scientific terms: late-night salivary cortisol (LNSC), free cortisol, circadian nadir, urine free cortisol, dexamethasone suppression test, meconium, fatty acid ethyl esters (FAEE), ethyl glucuronide (EtG), β1- and β2-transferrin, perilymph, vitreous humour, extravascular body fluid, matrix effect, method modification, verification and validation.
explanation.why: Free cortisol and unbound drugs cross into saliva, so saliva tracks the active fraction. Meconium forms once fetal swallowing begins and accumulates drug and alcohol metabolites, so it integrates later-pregnancy exposure. β2-transferrin is present in CSF but not in serum, tears or nasal secretions. Fluids differ from serum in pH, electrolytes, protein, lipid and viscosity, which can distort an assay designed for serum.
explanation.measure: LNSC: two separate evenings between 2300 and 2400 h; avoid smoking that day; steroid-containing lotions or oral gels can cause false positives and licorice may theoretically raise results; one of four initial tests; abnormal → endocrinologist and second test. Meconium: forms from about 12 weeks (some say up to 20); FAEE cumulative cut-point 2 nmol/g (one study: sensitivity 84.2%, specificity 83.3%); EtG ≥10 ng/g used for third-trimester exposure in one cohort. β2-transferrin: agarose electrophoresis with antitransferrin immunodetection on microlitre volumes. Matrix: validate (precision, trueness, reportable range, interferences/matrix effect) for each fluid type and assay; report with a limitation comment if a matrix effect cannot be excluded.
explanation.differs: Saliva (free cortisol) vs serum total cortisol; meconium (long window, later pregnancy, slow to obtain) vs neonatal urine (fast, recent use only); β2-transferrin (CSF, perilymph, vitreous) vs β1-transferrin (serum, tears, nasal secretions, saliva); verification of a manufacturer claim vs validation of an off-label fluid.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the correct LNSC collection time and its interferences, why a negative meconium does not exclude first-trimester exposure, which marker confirms CSF rhinorrhoea and its false positives, and what a lab must do before reporting a body-fluid result on a serum assay.

comparisons.title: Meconium vs neonatal urine

left.label: Meconium
points: Slow to obtain; may pass in utero

comparisons.distinguisher: Length of the exposure window vs speed of the answer.

comparisons.title: β1- vs β2-transferrin
comparisons.distinguisher: A β2 band in nasal or ear fluid points to CSF, unless vitreous humour or perilymph could explain it.

mnemonic.text: Every specimen is a witness with a window: saliva saw the FREE cortisol at bedtime; meconium saw the LATER months of pregnancy; β2-transferrin saw the fluid around the brain. No witness is believed until the lab has validated it.
mnemonic.explanation: Links each matrix to what and when it reports, and to the matrix-validation rule.
mnemonic.limitation: Meconium formation onset is debated (about 12–20 weeks), so its window has no sharp start; β2-transferrin is also in perilymph and vitreous humour; steroid lotions or oral gels can falsely raise salivary cortisol, and licorice may in theory do so.

analogyLimitations: Meconium marker cut-offs come from individual studies; laboratories and methods differ.
takeaway: Each alternative specimen has its own window, with saliva showing free cortisol late at night, meconium showing the later months of pregnancy and beta-2 transferrin marking spinal, ear or eye fluid, and none of them may borrow serum reference ranges without validation.

questions.stem: A patient is to be screened for Cushing syndrome with late-night salivary cortisol. Which collection plan follows the 2008 Endocrine Society guideline?

options.text: Saliva on two separate evenings between 2300 and 2400 h, avoiding smoking that day
options.rationale: Correct. The guideline asks for two late-evening samples on separate nights and advises avoiding smoking on the collection day.

options.text: One saliva sample collected at 0800 h
options.rationale: Incorrect. The test looks for loss of the late-night low point; a morning sample cannot show it, and two measurements are recommended.

options.text: One late-evening sample shortly after applying a steroid oral gel
options.rationale: Incorrect. Steroid lotions or oral gels contaminating the swab may cause false positives, and two samples are recommended.

options.text: A late-evening sample interpreted with the serum total cortisol reference range
options.rationale: Incorrect. Saliva reflects free cortisol, not total serum cortisol, so serum total cortisol ranges do not apply to it.

questions.stem: Clear fluid drips from the nose after a head injury. Immunodetection after electrophoresis shows β2-transferrin. Which situation could make this a false positive for CSF?

options.text: A ruptured eyeball releasing vitreous humour
options.rationale: Correct. β2-transferrin is also present in vitreous humour, so eye rupture can give a false-positive result.

options.text: Normal nasal secretions mixed with tears
options.rationale: Incorrect. Tears and nasal secretions carry β1-transferrin, not β2-transferrin.
Incorrect. Saliva contains β1-transferrin, not β2-transferrin.

options.text: A nasal glucose strip reading above 20 mg/dL
options.rationale: Incorrect. Glucose strips are a separate, less reliable test; they do not change the β2-transferrin result.

questions.stem: A clinician asks the chemistry lab to run pleural fluid on an assay whose manufacturer lists only serum and plasma. What is the appropriate laboratory approach?

options.text: Treat it as a method modification: validate the assay for that fluid type, document it, and add a limitation comment if a matrix effect cannot be excluded
options.rationale: Correct. Off-label fluids need validation for each fluid type and assay, and results with possible matrix effects are reported with a comment.

options.text: Run it and report against the serum reference interval
options.rationale: Incorrect. Fluid composition differs from serum, performance is not transferable without validation, and most fluids lack reference intervals.

options.text: Run it once against serum quality control and report if the control passes
options.rationale: Incorrect. A serum control passing does not show whether the fluid’s matrix affects the assay; validation, including matrix-effect checks, must use the fluid type itself.

options.text: Refuse every body fluid request permanently
options.rationale: Incorrect. Validated body-fluid testing is clinically useful; the issue is validation, not refusal.

claims.text: Saliva mirrors free blood cortisol; loss of late-night nadir; four initial tests; two evenings 2300–2400 h; smoking, steroid gels/lotions and (theoretically) licorice; abnormal → endocrinologist and second test.
Drugs in oral fluid are mainly the unbound fraction.
Meconium forms from about 12 weeks (some say up to 20); reflects second- and third-trimester exposure, not the first; neonatal urine shows only recent use; meconium caveats.
FAEE cut-point 2 nmol/g, sensitivity 84.2% and specificity 83.3%; EtG ≥10 ng/g as a third-trimester marker in one cohort.
β1 vs β2-transferrin distribution; electrophoresis with antitransferrin detection on microlitre volumes; false positive with eye rupture; costly and slow.
Off-label fluids are a method modification needing validation per fluid type and assay; matrix effect; limitation comment; viscosity and hyaluronidase pre-treatment.

Reviewer wording that meconium EtG “documents maternal alcohol use” in general; specific β2-transferrin sensitivity and specificity figures; the CLSI C49-A text itself; salivary cortisol as the single most sensitive screen.
claims.note: Not taught as facts in this lesson; C49-A was not read (not open access).

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 30 Hit 14 calls β2-transferrin CSF-specific. Oh 2017 still calls it highly sensitive and specific, but states it is also present in perilymph and vitreous humour and that eye rupture can produce a false positive; the lesson teaches this qualification (register flag rv-b2-transferrin-not-csf-only).

Ch. 30 Hit 12 gives meconium a 2nd–3rd trimester window, which is broadly consistent with the sources, but the onset is imprecise and the EtG statement is unqualified. Lange 2014 and Price 2018 place formation at about 12 weeks, with some authors suggesting up to 20 weeks; Maschke 2021 used meconium EtG ≥10 ng/g as a third-trimester marker; Price 2018 adds that meconium can be passed in utero or contain labour drugs. The lesson teaches the window with these qualifications (register flag rv-meconium-window-onset).
